stem: The first rule of performance work is:
options: MEASURE, never guess - intuition about what is slow is wrong more often than right
explanation: Write clearly, measure to find the real hot spot, fix the top item, measure again. Everything else follows.

options: A RELEASE build, a warm-up run (JIT compiles on first call), and repetition
explanation: Debug builds and cold JIT lie. For real work BenchmarkDotNet does warm-up and statistics; Stopwatch is the classroom tool for 2x-and-up effects.

stem: The hidden cost of allocating millions of objects is:
options: Future GARBAGE-COLLECTOR work - allocation is cheap, collection is the price (4.8)
explanation: Bump-a-pointer is fast; the pauses come later. Reducing allocations is the real lever, not micro-tuning arithmetic.

stem: object o = i; sum += (int)o; in a two-million loop is slow because:
options: Each iteration BOXES an int onto the heap - millions of tiny objects, streams of gen-0 collections
explanation: The measured cost, and 3.4's closing argument: generics exist so List<int> never boxes.

stem: s += "x" across 20,000 iterations is quadratic because:
options: Immutable strings mean each += COPIES everything so far into a new string (1.8)
explanation: StringBuilder keeps one growable buffer: ~1ms vs hundreds. Now with the mechanism, not just the rule.

stem: new List<int>(2_000_000) beats a default-capacity list because:
options: It SKIPS ~21 doublings, each of which copied the whole array (3.1)
explanation: The cheapest optimisation in the language - one constructor argument. List, Dictionary and StringBuilder all take a capacity.

stem: A million-element struct array builds ~5x faster than a class array because:
options: It is ONE allocation with values inline; the classes are 1,000,001 heap objects chased by reference (2.8)
explanation: Contiguous values love the CPU cache; scattered objects cause misses. Why Point-like types should be structs.

stem: Span<int> window = data.AsSpan(10, 10) differs from data[10..20] in that the span:
options: Is a VIEW over the same memory - no copy; writes go through to the array
explanation: Slicing without allocating - array, string, or stackalloc buffer. High-performance parsing lives on Span.

stem: "Premature optimisation is the root of all evil" means:
options: Clarity first; optimise the MEASURED hot spot - but it does NOT excuse an obvious O(n squared)
explanation: Choosing the right algorithm and collection is design, not premature anything. The quote targets unmeasured micro-tuning of cold code.

stem: The performance win that matters MOST, first:
options: The ALGORITHM - O(n squared) to O(n log n) beats every micro-tune (module 5)
explanation: Then the right collection (3.2), then fewer allocations, then batched I/O, and parallelism last. In that order.
